Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A round black-capped chickadee perched on an arching autumn branch, with four gold and red-orange leaves, in front of a misty forest at sunset.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

11 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The chickadee's head, black cap and bib, and eye, at about 48% across and 21% down in the frame. Light: The setting sun, upper right of the bird at 64% across and 14% down in the frame. It backlights the bird, so the chest on the right glows and the tops of the branches catch warm light.How this lesson was made

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: covering and blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: the sun diskRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: the soft trunksFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat or round bristle brush: dabbing the soft clumpsOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1/2 inch flat: the thick branchesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #4 round: the thin twigsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #8 round: the leaf shapesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #2 round: stems and veinsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch filbert or #10 round: the round body and the wingFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • Liner (#1 or #0): legs and toesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

STEP 1 OF 11

Blend the misty sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the setting sun, upper right: 67% across, 14% down. Every highlight goes on that side.
  2. Dab a Sun cream disk there, about 6% wide, with the #6 round.
  3. With the 1 inch flat, X-stroke Sunset gold around it, 30% to 90% across, top half. Blend Foliage rust into its left side, 15% to 35% across, 20% to 40% down.
  4. X-stroke Misty blue-gray down both sides and across the bottom, blending into the gold while wet.
  5. Work Mist gray into the lower right corner and the left middle, and tap a few gold spots low down. No white should show.
Paints for this step5 paints, 5 new
  • Misty blue-gray new2 parts violet, 2 parts white, 1 part cadmium green, a touch of cashew
  • Sunset gold new3 parts yellow deep, 2 parts white, 1 part light magenta
  • Sun cream new1 part white, a touch of cashew, a touch of yellow ochre
  • Foliage rust new2 parts raw sienna, 1 part light magenta, a touch of yellow deep
  • Mist gray new2 parts violet, 1 part cadmium green, 1 part white, a touch of raw umber

Colors dry a little darker, so test a mix on the palette edge before the big sky.

Mix plenty of the blue-gray; it covers most of the canvas.

Brushes

1 inch flat#6 round

Strokes

X stroke. Criss-cross the flat in overlapping X shapes, wet and creamy, so the gold and blue-gray melt together with soft texture.

Wet-on-wet blend. Where gold meets blue-gray, stroke lightly across the join while both are wet, then stop.

Watch out: Stop blending when the paint starts to drag; streaks look like mist.

Watch out: Don't stop at the branch line: the sky runs to the bottom edge.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Why this tool: The sky alone is the finish with every later layer removed; no filter can take away the bird, branches, and foliage and paint the sky behind them, and the composite tool (#8) doesn't exist yet.

No diagram: A blend: the words give where the gold and blue-gray go and where the sun sits.

STEP 2 OF 11

Paint the far misty trunks

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the 3/4 inch flat and Mist gray thinned a little with water, pull two tall trunks straight down the full height, one or two long strokes each: 85% to 90% across and 94% to 98%.
  3. Drag a thinner limb up and left off the first trunk, from 15% down to the top edge at 78% across.
  4. Dry-brush a paler third trunk at 82% to 85% across, from halfway down, and two short faint ones rising from the bottom at 37% and 44%.
Paints for this step1 paint
  • Mist gray from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts violet, 1 part cadmium green, 1 part white, a touch of raw umber

Try a dry-brush stroke on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.

Brushes

3/4 inch flat

Strokes

Long pull-down. Load the flat with thinned gray and pull straight down in one or two long strokes, so the trunk is solid but pale.

Dry brushing. Load the flat, wipe it almost dry on a towel, and drag it down lightly so the marks stay broken and see-through.

Watch out: Dark, sharp trunks look close. These are far away: pale and soft.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 11

Dab the hazy foliage, first pass

  1. Let the trunks dry.
  2. With the old stiff flat and a little Foliage rust, dab the biggest clump from 25% to 55% across, 15% to 50% down, and one below it at 40% to 57% across, 55% to 80% down.
  3. Add a band along the top from 60% to 85% across, a group around the right trunks, and a few low at the bottom left. Tap lightly so edges stay ragged.
  4. Wipe the brush and tap a few soft Misty blue-gray clumps at the upper left, down the lower left edge, and right of center low (63% to 80% across, 68% to 85% down).
Paints for this step2 paints
  • Foliage rust from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts raw sienna, 1 part light magenta, a touch of yellow deep
  • Misty blue-gray from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts violet, 2 parts white, 1 part cadmium green, a touch of cashew

Test the tap on scrap paper first.

Brushes

old stiff flat or round bristle brush

Strokes

Dabbing. Hold the stiff brush upright, nearly dry, and tap with the bristle tips; the marks get more solid the more you tap, so stop while sky still shows.

Watch out: Too much paint makes solid blobs. Wipe the brush on a towel before you tap.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 11

Dab light on the foliage

  1. Let the rust clumps dry.
  2. Tap Sunset gold on the upper sides of the clumps nearest the sun, between 30% and 90% across in the top half, fewer taps farther from the sun.
  3. Let the gold dry. Wipe the brush, then tap Misty blue-gray over the lower halves of the far clumps and the middle of the big center clump, so they turn hazy.
  4. Leave rust showing between the gold and gray. Add a few Foliage rust taps where a clump needs a darker bottom.

STEP 5 OF 11

Paint the branches dark

  1. Let the background dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat and creamy Bark brown, pull the main branch as in the diagram: from the bottom left corner up to its top at 59% down, 40% to 55% across.
  3. It's about 12% thick at the left and 5% under the bird, forks at 82% across, 73% down, and curves down to the right edge near the bottom.
  4. Pull the upright branch from the top edge (0% to 10% across) down into the main branch at 10% across, 67% down.
  5. With the #4 round, press and lift the thin twigs at the right and the one at the top, 15% across.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Bark brown new1 part raw umber, a touch of crimson, a touch of permanent black

Brushes

1/2 inch flat#4 round

Strokes

Thick-to-thin. Press the flat down for the thick part, then turn it onto its edge as you pull, so the branch tapers.

Press and lift. Press the round's belly at the twig's base and lift to the tip as you pull outward.

Watch out: An even, tube-like branch looks stiff. Thick at the left, thin at the right.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 11

Light the tops of the branches

  1. Let the dark branches dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat, nearly dry, drag Bark tan along the top edge of every branch, following its curve.
  3. Keep the tan on the top half, facing the sun, in long broken bands. The Bark brown stays on the undersides and in the gaps.
  4. Touch tan along the right side of the upright branch too.

STEP 7 OF 11

Paint the four leaves

  1. Let the branches dry.
  2. Leaf gold leaves: one at the top from 15% to 34% across, 0% to 12% down; one hanging under the branch from 48% to 65% across, 70% to 93% down.
  3. Leaf red leaves: one hanging from 8% to 22% across, 8% to 38% down; one from 66% to 80% across, 79% to 100% down.
  4. With the #8 round, build each leaf as in the diagram: a center stroke, then press-and-lift points on each side. Add a few strokes of the other leaf color inside.
  5. Once dry, pull a thin Bark brown stem and center vein with the #2 round.

  • Leaf gold newYellow deep, straight from the tube
  • Leaf red new1 part yellow deep, 1 part crimson, a touch of white
  • Bark brown from step 5, mix more if it has dried1 part raw umber, a touch of crimson, a touch of permanent black

It may look busy and unfinished right now. That's the ugly stage, and it's normal.

Brushes

#8 round#2 round

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the round's belly down and lift to the tip as you pull outward, making each jagged point of the leaf.

Liner work. Thin the brown to ink and pull the stem and vein in one steady stroke, over dry paint only.

Watch out: Round, smooth leaves. Let the points stay jagged.

Watch out: Yellow is see-through: paint the gold leaves, let them dry, and paint them again so no gray shows.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 11

Block in the bird's body

  1. Let the leaves dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch filbert and creamy Belly buff, paint the body as one big round: 37% to 60% across, 28% to 56% down.
  3. Add the head as a smaller round on top, up to 11% down, as in the diagram. Two coats.
  4. With the #6 round and Wing gray, paint the wing from 45% across, 28% down to 23% across, 48% down, then the tail to its tip at 14% across, 62% down.
  5. Once dry, paint a thin Bark brown shadow on the branch right under the belly, 41% to 60% across.

  • Wing gray new3 parts white, 2 parts permanent black, a touch of flesh tint
  • Bark brown from step 5, mix more if it has dried1 part raw umber, a touch of crimson, a touch of permanent black

Strokes

Building from pieces. Start with the big body oval, then add the head round on top and the wing and tail over the left side.

Watch out: A small head. The head is almost as wide as the top of the body.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 9 OF 11

Paint the cap, bib, and cheek

  1. Let the body dry.
  2. With the #6 round and Chickadee black, fill the cap over the top of the head, 38% to 56% across, 11% to 24% down, as in the diagram.
  3. Bring the black down the right side of the face into the bib under the beak, 46% to 58% across, 18% to 30% down.
  4. Let the black dry, then paint the Cheek white patch between them: 38% to 50% across, 22% to 29% down.

Brushes

#6 round

Strokes

Building from pieces. Cap first, then the bib joined to it on the right, then the white cheek fills the gap below the cap.

Watch out: White touching wet black turns gray. Wait for the black to dry.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 10 OF 11

Shade the feathers

  1. Let the head dry.
  2. With the #6 round, stroke Chest cream down the right side of the chest, 48% to 60% across, 28% to 50% down, curving with the round body.
  3. Stroke Belly shadow on the lower left of the belly, leaving the middle Belly buff. Flick short fluffy strokes along the body's edges.
  4. With the #2 round, pull Charcoal gray stripes along the wing and down the tail.
  5. Let the stripes dry, then edge the wing feathers with Wing gray.

Brushes

#6 round#2 round

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Pull each stroke in an arc around the round body: lighter mix on the sun side, darker on the far side.

Flicking. With a light load, flick short strokes outward from the body's edge for fluffy feathers.

Watch out: Straight strokes flatten the body. Curve every stroke around it.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 11 OF 11

Add the eye, beak, and feet

  1. Let everything dry.
  2. With the #2 round, dot the eye in Chickadee black at 47% across, 21% down, then a tiny Sun cream dot on its upper right.
  3. Paint the short pointed beak in Charcoal gray at 51% to 54% across, 18% to 20% down.
  4. With the liner and inky Charcoal gray, paint the two legs at 41% and 52% across, from the belly down to the branch, with toes curling around it.
Paints for this step3 paints
  • Chickadee black from step 9, mix more if it has dried1 part permanent black, a touch of raw umber, a touch of violet
  • Charcoal gray from step 10, mix more if it has dried3 parts permanent black, 1 part flesh tint, 1 part white, a touch of purple red
  • Sun cream from step 1, mix more if it has dried1 part white, a touch of cashew, a touch of yellow ochre

Test a liner line on scrap paper first. Then step back: stop before it feels done.

Brushes

#2 roundLiner (#1 or #0)

Strokes

Dotting. Touch the brush tip down once for the eye, and once more for the highlight after it dries.

Liner work. Thin the gray to ink and pull each toe in one short stroke, curving around the branch.

Watch out: A big eye. It's a small dot, about a quarter inch.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A black-capped chickadee on an autumn branch at sunset (a painting).

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, or page around it.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: about 21% of plain misty sky and foliage at the top and bottom

Why: The picture is square; landscape keeps the whole bird and the arching branch, and the frame's side bands were filled by one render (redone once because the first warmed every color).

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, dozens of thorny twigs and buds. Hundreds of items: yes, flaky bark chips and fluffy feather strokes. Detail inside big shapes: yes, the background trees and foliage. Parts: about 7, within the budget of 8.

Changed: Dropped the thorny twigs, buds, and small leaf clusters; merged the bark into long bands with a light top; merged the background into two or three soft trunks and a few loose foliage masses; smoothed the sky into blue-gray and gold around a soft sun; simplified the bird into soft masses; kept the four big leaves as simple shapes.

Why: A beginner can't paint hundreds of bark chips and twigs; the bird, branch, leaves, and sun are what the picture is recognized by.

A round chickadee on an arching branch, backlit by a low sun in a misty autumn forest. What matters is the bird's round shape and its black-and-white head pattern against the warm glow; what's hard is the original's fine detail (thorny twigs, flaky bark, a thousand fluffy feather strokes, busy foliage). The lesson should be about soft background layers, a branch with a lit top, and building a bird from a few round shapes.

Subject: A round black-capped chickadee perched on an arching autumn branch, with four gold and red-orange leaves, in front of a misty forest at sunset.
Focal point: The chickadee's head, black cap and bib, and eye, at about 48% across and 21% down in the frame.
Light: The setting sun, upper right of the bird at 64% across and 14% down in the frame. It backlights the bird, so the chest on the right glows and the tops of the branches catch warm light.

What it saw, back to front

  1. misty sky and sunset glow with the sun
  2. far misty tree trunks
  3. hazy background foliage (rust, then gold)
  4. branches (dark, then light bark)
  5. four leaves
  6. bird body, wing, and tail
  7. bird head markings
  8. bird feather values
  9. eye, beak, and feet
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint along, back to front fits a scene with a soft background, a branch in front of it, and one subject in front of that: sky, far trunks, foliage, branches, leaves, then the bird in base, markings, and shading, the way YouTube beginner tutorials paint a bird on a branch.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

It starts with a toned ground and a sketch; the owner follows paint-along tutorials, and this picture's misty sky works best painted straight onto white with wet blending.

How the paint recipes were worked out16 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order11 steps

Back to front: the sky first, run to every edge; then the far misty trunks, then the foliage in two passes (dark, then light) so the texture builds up; then the branches, dark then lit tops; the leaves hang in front of the background; then the bird in a teacher's three layers (flat shapes, head markings, values), and the eye, beak, and feet last.

  1. 1. Blend the misty sunset sky

    Everything else sits on it, so it goes first and covers the whole canvas, blended wet in one go.

  2. 2. Paint the far misty trunks

    The farthest solid things, painted soft over the dry sky before any foliage overlaps them.

  3. 3. Dab the hazy foliage, first pass

    The darker first pass of the hazy foliage, so no step jumps from flat sky to finished clumps.

  4. 4. Dab light on the foliage

    The light pass on the clumps nearest the sun, leaving the rust underneath.

  5. 5. Paint the branches dark

    The branch is in front of the whole background and behind the bird, so it goes on once the background is dry, as one flat dark shape.

  6. 6. Light the tops of the branches

    The lit top of the branch gives it roundness; it's its own pass over the dry dark base.

  7. 7. Paint the four leaves

    The leaves hang in front of the background and branch and don't touch the bird, so they go before the subject.

  8. 8. Block in the bird's body

    The subject's base shapes, as a teacher blocks them in: one round body, the head on top, wing and tail over it.

  9. 9. Paint the cap, bib, and cheek

    The black-and-white head pattern is what makes it a chickadee; it goes on the dry base, cap first.

  10. 10. Shade the feathers

    The values that make the bird round: the sun-lit chest, a darker far side, and wing stripes.

  11. 11. Add the eye, beak, and feet

    The smallest marks last: eye, beak, and feet.

Filters it tried13 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams4 steps, free

Four steps add a shaped thing whose construction the picture doesn't show: the branches, the leaves, the bird's body, and the head markings. The rest are blends, repeated dabs, or small marks the words place.

  • Step 5: Paint the branches dark beginner check

    Noticed: Where the upright branch joins the main arch, and how thick the arch is from end to end, isn't clear from a picture of finished bark.

    Pieces: The main arch first as one tapered shape, then the upright branch down into it, then the twigs, biggest to smallest, drawn at the canvas's real 14 x 11 shape.

  • Step 7: Paint the four leaves beginner check

    Noticed: The leaf outline is jagged, with repeated points; a beginner wouldn't know how to get it with a round brush.

    Pieces: A center stroke, then press-and-lift points on each side angled outward, then the stem and vein once dry.

  • Step 8: Block in the bird's body beginner check

    Noticed: The bird appears whole in one step; the chubby body, head, wing, and tail are hard to place freehand.

    Pieces: One big body oval, a round head on top almost as wide, then the wing as a slanted oval over the left side and the tail as a long wedge down to the left, the way a teacher draws a chickadee.

  • Step 9: Paint the cap, bib, and cheek beginner check

    Noticed: Where the black cap ends and how it joins the bib is the chickadee's marking, and the first renders got it wrong, so the painter needs it shown.

    Pieces: The cap over the top first, then the black running down the right side into the bib, then the white cheek filling the gap below the cap.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A blend: the words give where the gold and blue-gray go and where the sun sits.
  • Step 2: Straight soft vertical strokes at given positions.
  • Step 3: Repeated dabs; the picture shows where.
  • Step 4: Repeated taps on the tops of existing clumps.
  • Step 6: One dry-brush stroke along the top of shapes already painted.
  • Step 10: Curved strokes on a shape already built; the values table and picture show where each value goes.
  • Step 11: Three small marks placed by grid numbers.
What the reviewer caught31 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check The first finish turned the soft, muted blue-gray mist of the beginner version into bright saturated cornflower blue, made the far trunks blue instead of gray, and gave the background foliage hard, saturated edges, so the misty sunset mood was gone. Repainted once with those fixes; the repaint matches.
  • Round 1 Step 3: The warm golden glow through the middle of the sky (35% to 75% across, 35% to 75% down) was repainted as blue-gray haze in a step that only adds rust foliage; the glow is back in the next step and the finish. (redone)
  • Round 1 Step 4: Adds whole new golden clumps across the center (35% to 75% across, 30% to 75% down) with no rust underneath, and faint trunks no step paints. (redone neighbor foliage-rust: the center clumps are in the finish, so the rust pass was missing them; the redo of foliage-rust paints their rust base, and the gold step now adds light on top of them)
  • Round 1 Step 7: The four leaves were flat single-color shapes, but from the bird-body step to the finish they have brushy two-tone shading that no step paints. (redone)
  • Round 1 Step 10: The white cheek ran across the whole face and separated the cap from the bib; in the finish the cap runs down the right side of the face to join the bib. The bird-head step had the same mismatch. (redone (bird-head redone with the same fix))
  • Round 2 Step 9: The glowing cream chest on the right side of the body showed up already in the head step; it belongs to the feather step. (redone)

  • Text check: missing Step 2: A limb forking up-left off the first trunk and a third faint trunk weren't in the text. (fixed)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The canvas-fill render with the default prompt warmed the whole picture; asking it to keep every color and not make it warmer fixed it in one try.
  • The first finish turned soft mist into bright saturated blue; naming the mist as muted and dusty in the repaint fixed it.
  • Rendered steps added the bird's chest glow a step early and drew the cheek across the whole face; the head markings needed exact measured boxes in the fix.
  • Section 6a's from-finish makes a recut copy, which can't be sealed hands-off, so this run planned foliage passes over the sky instead of a base coat plus passes and relied on texture_jumps (which came back empty).
  • The research notes don't cover painting birds or feathers; the bird's construction (body oval, head, wing, tail) and the cap-bib-cheek order came from general drawing practice, not the cited notes.
  • The step reviewer flagged only the bark step shortening a limb, but its sheet showed the flat branches step had a different branch thickness and bend from the finish; checking a flagged pair against the finish caught it, and one --fix redo of each fixed it.
  • The step reviewer proposed splitting the feather step (shading, then wing stripes); it was left as one step because only a texture jump can be split for free, and new renders were not worth the redo budget.
